growth_story.headline: Oil made Equatorial Guinea one of Africa's fastest-growing economies; as its fields aged, income per person fell to 65.5 percent below its 2008 peak.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in Equatorial Guinea grew by 29.9 percent a year over 1990–2001, as large oil reserves found in the 1990s made the country one of Sub-Saharan Africa's biggest oil producers. Growth slowed to 10.4 percent a year in 2002–2009, still carried by oil and, from 2008, by large infrastructure projects, and income per person peaked in 2008. Since 2010 it has fallen by 6.1 percent a year on average, as oil revenues dropped after the 2014 price crash and output from maturing fields declined from 2015. The economy outside oil and gas was too small and too narrow to fill the gap, and investment fell from 53.6 percent of GDP in 2009 to 6.4 percent in 2025. By 2025 income per person was 65.5 percent below its 2008 peak, about where it first was in 2001.

threads.text: Large oil finds in the 1990s turned a shrinking economy into one of the region's fastest growers. Income per person grew by 140.5 percent in 1997 alone, and growth averaged 29.9 percent a year over 1990–2001.

growth_story.tension: The sources date the end of the oil boom to 2014 and the fall in oil output to 2015. In the data, income per person peaked in 2008 and fell by 13.0 percent in 2010, while investment was still 46.6 percent of GDP in 2012. The sources do not explain this earlier turn.
